case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Weaver v. Roanoke Department of Human Resources
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed the termination of both parents' residual parental rights because the record contained no evidence that social agencies made the 'reasonable and appropriate efforts' that Code § 16.1-283(C)(2) requires before rights may be severed, and directed that termination statutes be read to preserve the parent-child relationship where possible.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the constraint on court-ordered service plans: the plan and the efforts behind it must appear in the record or termination cannot follow.
key_cases.quote: Statutes terminating the legal relationship between parent and child should be interpreted consistently with the governmental objective of preserving, when possible, the parent-child relationship.

key_cases.case_name: Richardson v. Henry County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B)(2), holding that proof that the mother without good cause failed to respond to available and reasonable rehabilitative efforts is statutory prima facie evidence of the (B)(2) conditions, which the mother then failed to rebut.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Virginia authority on how a parent's non-response to a court-supervised service regime shifts the burden of going forward.
key_cases.quote: Under the statute, this is prima facie evidence of the conditions set forth in subparagraph (B)(2) of the statute.

key_cases.case_name: Patricia Tackett v. Arlington County Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination of the mother's rights and denial of the grandmother's custody petition, holding that a relative lacks standing to assert the parent's rights and may appeal only the permanency-goal findings and the disposition of her own custody petition.
key_cases.relevance: The grandmother's failure to complete the psychological evaluation and employment verification required by the foster care plan is what defeated her custody petition.
key_cases.quote: Grandmother only has standing to appeal the circuit court’s findings made in connection with the change in permanency goal and with regard to grandmother’s petition for custody.

key_cases.case_name: Berrien v. Greene County Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed an order terminating a mother's parental rights and entered final judgment restoring custody to her, holding that even though credible evidence supported the trial court's best-interests finding, the Department bore and failed to carry the burden of proving parental unfitness before rights could be permanently terminated.
key_cases.relevance: The juvenile court had awarded the mother custody on a court-supervised 'probationary period of indeterminate length' to verify she was providing a suitable home, and the Court measured the Department's case against what that supervision actually produced.
key_cases.quote: the burden was on the Department to prove Berrien's unfitness before the trial court could take the ultimate, drastic, and irrevocable step of permanently terminating her parental rights

key_cases.case_name: Toms v. Hanover Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that rehabilitative services are a relevant concern but not an absolute prerequisite to a subsection (B) termination and that due process imposes no constitutional duty to provide them, while distinguishing subsection (C), which turns on the parent's failure to remedy problems during a period in which services were offered.
key_cases.relevance: Counsel litigating the adequacy of a court-approved service record must first identify which subsection is in play, because only subsection (C) measures the parent's response to the services actually offered.
key_cases.quote: subsection C requires the court to determine whether the parent has been unwilling or unable to remedy the problems during the period in which he has been offered rehabilitation services

key_cases.case_name: Fields v. Dinwiddie County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination entered under both Code § 16.1-283(C)(2) and § 16.1-283(E)(i), holding that an (E)(i) termination requires clear and convincing proof that termination is in the child's best interests together with a finding that the parent's rights to a sibling were previously terminated, which substitutes for proof that the parent failed to remedy the conditions leading to foster care.
key_cases.relevance: It shows that where a parent's rights to a sibling have already been terminated, the sufficiency of the current court-approved service plan and the parent's response to it drop out of the Department's case entirely.
key_cases.quote: In addition, the trial court must find the parent's rights to a sibling of the child previously had been terminated.
